summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a web tool for seeing how any patch of sky changes between SPHEREx visits. You type a name or coordinates (or put them in the URL). The tool finds every SPHEREx image that covers that position, removes the sky background, aligns the images on one grid, and stacks them into a single frame per visit, about six months apart. It then plays the frames as a short loop, the way Clyde Tombaugh blinked two plates to find Pluto.

Barnard's Star steps north by about ten arcseconds a year. Epsilon Indi B slides east. R Draconis loses two thirds of its brightness in twelve months. You can also subtract one visit from another, colour each visit differently in one still image, view each of the six detectors separately, overlay Gaia stars moved to the date of each frame, and click any pixel to get its 0.75 to 5 micron spectrum.

SPHEREx will image over a billion objects. Volunteers found most known brown dwarfs by blinking WISE images. This gives them the same instrument for SPHEREx.
details:
What it does

Enter a position in any common format: an object name, decimal degrees, or hours/degrees with colons or letters. The same values work in the address bar (?ra=269.446&dec=4.768&fov=180), so a view can be linked or embedded.

For that position the tool:

  1. Asks NASA's IRSA archive which SPHEREx Level-2 exposures contain the point. Barnard's Star has 358.
  2. Reads only the rows it needs from each 66 MB exposure in NASA's public cloud copy of the data, instead of downloading whole files.
  3. Subtracts the zodiacal light model and the remaining sky level, and masks pixels the mission flagged as bad.
  4. Reprojects each piece onto a north-up grid centred on the target and averages them with inverse-variance weights. Exposures more than 60 days apart go into separate frames.
  5. Sends the frames to the browser as raw numbers, so changing the brightness scale, blinking and subtracting are instant.

Views

  • Blink: the frames as a loop, with play, speed, zoom, and a film strip of every visit.
  • Difference: one visit minus another. A star that moved becomes a red and blue pair.
  • Sum: all visits added together for a deeper image.
  • Time colour: first visit in red, last in blue, in one still picture. Anything that stayed put is white.
  • Side by side: blink and difference together.

Using the 102 bands

Every SPHEREx exposure sees a given star at a different wavelength. The tool can stack each of the six detector arrays separately, or make a three-colour image from short, middle and long wavelengths. Clicking a pixel collects its brightness from every exposure and plots a spectrum from 0.75 to 5 microns, one curve per visit, with error bars and a CSV download. The same points become a light curve in any band.

Other data on top

Gaia DR3 stars are drawn where their proper motion puts them on the date of each frame, and a marker shows where the target itself should be. A panel shows the same field in 2MASS, WISE and DSS through Aladin Lite. A list of difference-image sources with no Gaia star at that position points to things worth a second look. Each frame lists the exposures that went into it, their wavelengths and the fraction of flagged pixels.

Results on the test targets

  • Barnard's Star: moves 9.5 arcseconds between the first and third visit. Gaia predicts 10.2.
  • Epsilon Indi B: four visits, clear motion in the predicted direction.
  • RW Aurigae: brightness near 4 microns drops by almost half in a year.
  • R Draconis: fades about threefold from June 2025 to June 2026. Its core saturates the detector, so the tool measures the surrounding halo and labels the result as relative.

Why it matters

Most known brown dwarfs were found by volunteers blinking WISE images in a browser. SPHEREx adds a spectrum for every pixel, but until now there was no way to simply look at a position and see what changed. This tool needs no install and no login. A researcher can check an object in a minute, a student can watch a star move, and a volunteer can hunt for something new.

What is creative about it

  • Time colour is an old photographic-plate trick applied to a new survey.
  • The spectrum comes for free from the same exposures that build the image.
  • Reading slices of files from the cloud makes an interactive tool possible on a laptop.
  • The start page is a celestial globe you can turn, with the test targets at their real positions.
  • The tool shows missing, saturated and undetected data as exactly that.

What I considered

  • SPHEREx pixels are 6 arcseconds across, so even the fastest star moves less than one pixel per visit. That is why alignment, a shared brightness scale and difference images matter more than raw resolution.
  • New releases: visits are found from observation dates at query time. Adding a release is one line of configuration.
  • Archive outages: results are cached on disk, and the five test targets keep working if the archive search is down.
  • Field of view from 1 to 30 arcminutes. Larger fields take longer to fetch.

Built with

Python, FastAPI, astropy, reproject, numpy and scipy on the server. Plain JavaScript and canvas in the browser, with no framework and no build step. pytest and Playwright for testing. Docker for packaging. I am a team of one and used Claude Code (Anthropic) as a coding assistant throughout.
